name: Dilophosaurus wetherilli
dietDetails: Preyed upon fish, small dinosaurs, and early herbivorous reptiles.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Northern Arizona by Jesse Williams in 1942. Named Dilophosaurus in 1970 by Samuel Paul Welles.
interestingFacts: {"Made famous by Jurassic Park, but the real animal was much larger, did not spit venom, and lacked a neck frill.","The twin crests on its skull were paper-thin and likely used for species recognition and courtship displays.","Its jaw was loosely connected near the front, which may have allowed it to catch fish or hook prey."}
sizeNotes: Grew up to 6 meters (20 feet) long, weighing about 400 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Welles, S.P. (1954). New Jurassic dinosaur from the Kayenta formation of Arizona. Bulletin of the Geological Society of America 65: 591–598.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38641"},{"citation":"Marsh, A.D. and Rowe, T.B. (2020). A comprehensive anatomical revision of Dilophosaurus wetherilli. Journal of Paleontology 94(S78): 1–60.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/jpa.2020.14"}]

name: Stegosaurus stenops
nameMeaning: Roof lizard with a narrow face
dietDetails: Low-lying plants, mosses, ferns, horsetails, and cycads.
discoveryHistory: First found in Colorado in 1877 by M.P. Felch. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh during the famous Bone Wars.
interestingFacts: {"Had 17 flat bony plates on its back that were not used for armor but likely for display or temperature regulation.","Its tail weapon, consisting of 4 long spikes, is formally called a 'thagomizer' (a term coined in a Far Side cartoon).","Its brain was famously tiny, about the size of a walnut, weighing only 80 grams."}
sizeNotes: Large individuals reached up to 9 meters in length and up to 7 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1887). Principal characters of American Jurassic dinosaurs. Part IX. The Stegosauria. American Journal of Science 34: 413–417.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38810"},{"citation":"Maidment, S.C.R. et al. (2008). Systematics and phylogeny of Stegosauria. Journal of Systematic Palaeontology 6(4): 367–407.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/S1477201908002459"}]

name: Brachiosaurus altithorax
nameMeaning: Arm lizard with a deep chest
dietDetails: High canopy conifers, ginkgos, and tree ferns.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in the Grand River Valley, Colorado, by Elmer Riggs in 1900. Described in 1903.
interestingFacts: {"Its front legs were longer than its hind legs, giving its back a sloping profile similar to a giraffe.","Unlike other sauropods, it held its neck nearly vertically to reach high-altitude vegetation.","Had massive, chisel-like teeth to crop leaves from tall branches without chewing them."}
sizeNotes: Length estimates range from 18 to 22 meters; weight ranges from 28 to 58 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Riggs, E.S. (1903). Brachiosaurus altithorax, the largest known dinosaur. American Journal of Science 15(88): 299–306.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38685"},{"citation":"Taylor, M.P. (2009). A re-evaluation of Brachiosaurus altithorax Riggs 1903 (Dinosauria: Sauropoda). Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology 29(3): 787–806.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/039.029.0301"}]

name: Allosaurus fragilis
dietDetails: Medium to large herbivorous dinosaurs like Stegosaurus and sauropods.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/55/Allosaurus_BW_mirrored.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Rlevente, original author: Nobu Tamura (CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAllosaurus_BW_mirrored.jpg"},{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fe/Allosaurus_Jaws_Steveoc86.jpg","type":"photo","credit":"Fossil jaw specimen photo","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Allosaurus_Jaws_Steveoc86.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory: First described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877 based on fragmentary remains from Colorado. Dozens of individuals were later found at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
interestingFacts: {"The most common large predator of Late Jurassic North America, accounting for a vast majority of theropod fossils found.","Its skull was highly flexible and could expand laterally, allowing it to swallow large chunks of meat.","Had a lower bite force than modern lions, suggesting it used its skull like an axe to slash at prey."}
sizeNotes: Average length was 8.5 meters (28 feet), but rare large specimens (like Saurophaganax) reached 11-12 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1877). Notice of new dinosaurian reptiles from the Jurassic formation. American Journal of Science 14: 514–516.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38596"}]

name: Archaeopteryx lithographica
nameMeaning: Ancient wing from the lithographic limestone
dietDetails: Insects, small lizards, and early mammals.
discoveryHistory: First fossil (a single feather) discovered in 1860 in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany. The famous London Specimen was found in 1861.
interestingFacts: {"Famous transitional fossil representing the link between non-avian theropod dinosaurs and modern birds.","Had flight feathers like a bird, but retained reptilian features: a long bony tail, three clawed fingers, and a jaw with teeth.","Its discovery occurred just two years after Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species', serving as key evidence."}
sizeNotes: Roughly the size of a modern common raven or magpie, weighing 0.5 to 1.0 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"von Meyer, H. (1861). Archaeopteryx lithographica aus dem lithographischen Schiefer von Solnhofen. Neues Jahrbuch für Mineralogie, Geognosie, Geologie und Petrefaktenkunde: 678–679.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=39327"}]

name: Yi qi
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, insects, and soft plant matter in forest canopies.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a farmer in Hebei Province, China. Described in 2015 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
interestingFacts: {"Had bat-like wings made of a membranous skin stretched between long fingers and a unique bony rod (styliform element).","One of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs, adapting to an arboreal, gliding lifestyle.","Its plumage preserved melanosomes, suggesting it had black and brown coloration."}
sizeNotes: Wingspan was around 60 cm; weighed roughly 380 grams.
sources: [{"citation":"Xu, X. et al. (2015). A bizarre Jurassic theropod dinosaur with membranous wings. Nature 521(7550): 70–73.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14423"}]

name: Ceratosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Described by O.C. Marsh in 1884 based on a nearly complete skeleton from Colorado.
• A notable specimen was found in the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry.
• Fossils have been discovered in North America, with possible remains in Portugal and Tanzania.
interestingFacts: ["It had a prominent horn on its snout.","Ceratosaurus possessed osteoderms along its back.","It likely competed with Allosaurus for prey."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ceratosaurus nasicornis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratosaurus"}]

name: Megalosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• The first genus of non-avian dinosaur to be validly named (1824 by William Buckland).
• Early discoveries in Oxfordshire, England, were initially interpreted as giant lizards.
• It became a 'wastebasket taxon' in the 19th and 20th centuries for many unclassified theropods.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'Great Lizard'.","It was one of the original three genera used to define 'Dinosauria'.","True Megalosaurus fossils are only known from the Middle Jurassic of England."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Megalosaurus bucklandii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalosaurus"}]

name: Cryolophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1990-91 during a field expedition in Antarctica led by William Hammer.
• Officially named in 1994, it was the first meat-eating dinosaur found in Antarctica.
• Additional material was recovered during subsequent expeditions in the 2000s.
interestingFacts: ["Known as 'Elvisaurus' due to its pompadour-like crest.","It lived in a relatively temperate Antarctic climate.","It is the largest known Early Jurassic theropod."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cryolophosaurus ellioti description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryolophosaurus"}]

name: Monolophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1981 by a Canadian-Chinese expedition in Xinjiang, China.
• Described and named in 1993 by Zhao Xijin and Philip J. Currie.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton with an articulated skull.
interestingFacts: ["It had a single large crest running down the midline of its snout.","The crest was heavily pneumatized (hollow).","It lived in an environment with deep lakes and rivers."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Monolophosaurus jiangi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monolophosaurus"}]

name: Torvosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1972 by Jim Jensen and Kenneth Stadtman in Colorado.
• Described in 1979 by Peter Galton and Jensen.
• A second species, T. gurneyi, was later identified from Portugal.
interestingFacts: ["It was one of the largest predators of its time.","It had exceptionally powerful jaws and large teeth.","Torvosaurus competed with Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus in the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Torvosaurus tanneri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torvosaurus"}]

name: Ornitholestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1900 at the Bone Cabin Quarry in Wyoming.
• Described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1903.
• Only one nearly complete skeleton is known.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'bird robber'.","It was a small, fast, and agile predator.","Contrary to early restorations, it likely did not have a horn on its nose."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ornitholestes hermanni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornitholestes"}]

name: Compsognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• The first specimen was discovered in the 1850s in the Solnhofen limestone of Germany.
• A larger, second specimen was found in France in 1971.
• It was historically considered the smallest known dinosaur for over a century.
interestingFacts: ["It was a very small, bipedal carnivore.","Its fossils were found with the remains of small lizards in their stomachs.","It lived on an archipelago in a shallow tropical sea."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Compsognathus longipes description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compsognathus"}]

name: Guanlong
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2000 in the Junggar Basin, Xinjiang, China.
• Named in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Two specimens, an adult and a juvenile, were found together.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest known tyrannosauroids.","It possessed a large, fragile crest on its head.","Its name means 'crowned dragon'."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Guanlong wucaii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanlong"}]

name: Proceratosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1910 in Gloucestershire, England.
• Initially thought to be an ancestor of Ceratosaurus (hence the name) when described in 1926.
• In 2010, it was reclassified as an early tyrannosauroid.
interestingFacts: ["It possessed a small crest on its snout.","It is one of the oldest known members of the tyrannosaur lineage.","Only a partial skull has been found."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Proceratosaurus bradleyi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceratosaurus"}]

name: Metriacanthosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 19th century in the Oxford Clay of England.
• Originally classified as a species of Megalosaurus in 1923.
• Alick Walker established the genus Metriacanthosaurus in 1964.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'moderately-spined lizard'.","It had tall neural spines on its back, though not forming a full sail.","It was a medium-sized apex predator of its ecosystem."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Metriacanthosaurus parkeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metriacanthosaurus"}]

name: Eustreptospondylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 1871 in a clay pit near Oxford, England.
• It was shuffled between several genera, including Megalosaurus, before Alick Walker named it in 1964.
• It remains one of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Europe.
interestingFacts: ["It lived in an island environment.","It may have scavenged marine carcasses that washed ashore.","The single known specimen is considered a subadult."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Eustreptospondylus oxoniensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustreptospondylus"}]

name: Piatnitzkysaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1977 by José Bonaparte in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Argentina.
• Described in 1979 as an early allosauroid or megalosauroid.
• Two partial skeletons are known.
interestingFacts: ["It was a medium-sized bipedal predator.","It represents one of the few known Middle Jurassic theropods from South America.","It shares primitive traits with basal tetanurans."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Piatnitzkysaurus floresi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piatnitzkysaurus"}]

name: Marshosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1976 at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
• Named by James Madsen in 1976 in honor of O.C. Marsh.
• Known from sparse, fragmentary remains.
interestingFacts: ["It was a medium-sized predator in the Morrison Formation.","It was rarer than competitors like Allosaurus.","Its exact taxonomic position within tetanurans is debated."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Marshosaurus bicentesimus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshosaurus"}]

name: Stokesosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1974 at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry, Utah.
• Named by James Madsen after geologist William Lee Stokes.
• Primarily known from a pair of distinct ilia (pelvic bones).
interestingFacts: ["It is an early member of the tyrannosauroid family.","It was a small, agile predator.","Similar fossils found in England were later reclassified as a separate genus, Juratyrant."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Stokesosaurus clevelandi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokesosaurus"}]

name: Tanycolagreus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1995 at the Bone Cabin Quarry West in Wyoming.
• Originally thought to be Coelurus, it was named as a new genus in 2005.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skull and skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'long-limbed hunter'.","It was slightly larger and more robust than its relative Ornitholestes.","It had a long, low skull compared to other small theropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Tanycolagreus topwilsoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanycolagreus"}]

name: Sciurumimus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in a limestone quarry in Bavaria, Germany.
• Described in 2012 by Oliver Rauhut and colleagues.
• The single specimen is an exceptionally preserved juvenile.
interestingFacts: ["The fossil preserves filamentous feathers, especially along the tail.","Its name means 'squirrel mimic' due to its bushy tail.","Initially thought to be a megalosauroid, it may be a primitive coelurosaur."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sciurumimus albersdoerferi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciurumimus"}]

name: Juravenator
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1998 in the Solnhofen limestone in Germany.
• Named in 2006 by Ursula Göhlich and Luis Chiappe.
• The specimen is a nearly complete juvenile skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Its fossil shows patches of scaly skin, suggesting a lack of feathers in some areas.","It had unusually large eyes, suited for nocturnal hunting.","It was a very small, agile predator."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Juravenator starki description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juravenator"}]

name: Diplodocus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1877 in Colorado by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Williston.
• Described by O.C. Marsh in 1878.
• The famous 'Dippy' cast is based on a specimen found in 1899 in Wyoming.
interestingFacts: ["It had an exceptionally long, whip-like tail.","Its center of gravity allowed it to rear up on its hind legs.","Its teeth were peg-like and restricted to the front of the jaw."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Diplodocus carnegii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplodocus"}]

name: Apatosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered and named by O.C. Marsh in 1877 in Colorado.
• For over a century, its skeleton was mounted with the wrong skull (that of a Camarasaurus).
• A correct skull was finally mounted on skeletons in the late 1970s.
interestingFacts: ["It had a very robust, heavily built skeleton compared to Diplodocus.","Its tail may have been able to crack like a whip, producing a loud sound.","It was an abundant herbivore in the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Apatosaurus ajax description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apatosaurus"}]

name: Brontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Named by O.C. Marsh in 1879 from a specimen found at Como Bluff, Wyoming.
• In 1903, it was synonymized with Apatosaurus and the name fell out of formal use.
• A comprehensive study in 2015 reinstated Brontosaurus as a valid, separate genus.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'thunder lizard'.","It had a slightly thinner and less robust neck than Apatosaurus.","It is one of the most culturally famous dinosaur names."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Brontosaurus excelsus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brontosaurus"}]

name: Camarasaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1877 in Colorado by Oramel W. Lucas.
• Named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
• It is the most common sauropod found in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: ["It had a boxy, blunt skull with large, spoon-shaped teeth.","Its name means 'chambered lizard', referring to hollow chambers in its vertebrae.","It likely fed on tough, fibrous vegetation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Camarasaurus supremus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camarasaurus"}]

name: Giraffatitan
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania between 1909 and 1912.
• Originally described as a species of Brachiosaurus (B. brancai) in 1914 by Werner Janensch.
• Elevated to its own genus, Giraffatitan, by Gregory S. Paul in 1988.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the tallest known dinosaurs.","A famous, nearly complete skeleton is mounted in the natural history museum in Berlin.","It was adapted for high-browsing on conifer trees."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Giraffatitan brancai description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giraffatitan"}]

name: Barosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by early bone hunters for O.C. Marsh in South Dakota in 1889.
• Named in 1890, though more complete remains were found later in Utah.
• Remains have also been controversially attributed to it from Tanzania.
interestingFacts: ["It is closely related to Diplodocus but had a significantly longer neck.","Its neck vertebrae were exceptionally elongated.","A famous mount at the AMNH shows it rearing up to defend against an Allosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Barosaurus lentus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barosaurus"}]

name: Dicraeosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during the German Tendaguru expeditions in Tanzania (1909–1912).
• Described by Werner Janensch in 1914.
• Multiple specimens have been recovered, making it well-understood.
interestingFacts: ["It had tall, bifurcated (Y-shaped) neural spines on its neck and back.","It had a relatively short neck for a sauropod.","It was a low-browser in an ecosystem dominated by taller sauropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dicraeosaurus hansemanni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicraeosaurus"}]

name: Omeisaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1939 in Sichuan, China.
• Named by C.C. Young in 1939 after Mount Omei.
• Massive bonebeds in the Dashanpu Quarry have yielded numerous skeletons.
interestingFacts: ["It had a long, heavily built neck.","Some species assigned to it may have had a tail club.","It was a common large herbivore in its ecosystem."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Omeisaurus junghsiensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omeisaurus"}]

name: Vulcanodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1969 on an island in Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe.
• Described by Michael Raath in 1972.
• Originally thought to be a prosauropod due to associated carnivore teeth, later recognized as scavenged.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest known true sauropods.","Its forelimbs retained some primitive traits while its hindlimbs were column-like.","It lived in a volcanic landscape."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Vulcanodon karibaensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanodon"}]

name: Patagosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 1970s in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Argentina.
• Described by José Bonaparte in 1979.
• Remains of at least six individuals were found together, suggesting gregarious behavior.
interestingFacts: ["It was a basal eusauropod with a relatively short neck.","Adults and juveniles were found together, indicating herd living.","It was a dominant herbivore in its South American ecosystem."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Patagosaurus fariasi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagosaurus"}]

name: Cetiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in England and named by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It was the very first sauropod ever discovered and named.
• Originally, Owen believed it was a giant marine crocodile, hence the name 'whale lizard'.
interestingFacts: ["Its vertebrae lacked the complex hollow air sacs seen in later sauropods.","It was a primitive sauropod weighing roughly 15 tons.","It serves as an important baseline for understanding early sauropod evolution."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cetiosaurus oxoniensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetiosaurus"}]

name: Spinophorosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in Niger by a Spanish-German expedition.
• Described in 2009 by Remes and colleagues.
• The holotype is one of the most complete basal sauropod skeletons ever found.
interestingFacts: ["It originally was thought to have a spiked tail club (thagomizer), but the spikes were later re-identified as collarbones.","It is one of the best-preserved early sauropods.","Its anatomy provides a crucial link between basal sauropodomorphs and eusauropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Spinophorosaurus nigerensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinophorosaurus"}]

name: Haplocanthosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1901 by William H. Utterback in Colorado.
• Named by John Bell Hatcher in 1903.
• Known from a few incomplete specimens in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: ["It is considered a primitive macronarian sauropod.","It lacked the extreme specialized features of Diplodocus or Camarasaurus.","It was one of the smaller sauropods of the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Haplocanthosaurus priscus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplocanthosaurus"}]

name: Supersaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1972 by Jim Jensen at the Dry Mesa Quarry in Colorado.
• Named in 1985 based on massive, isolated bones.
• More complete remains found in Wyoming in 1996 confirmed its distinct genus status.
interestingFacts: ["It is among the longest dinosaurs ever discovered.","It was a diplodocid, closely related to Apatosaurus.","Its neck vertebrae were exceptionally elongated and robust."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Supersaurus vivianae description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersaurus"}]

name: Suuwassea
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 in Montana by a University of Pennsylvania expedition.
• Named in 2004 by J.D. Harris and Peter Dodson.
• The name comes from a Native American word meaning 'ancient thunder'.
interestingFacts: ["It is a primitive member of the dicraeosaurid family.","It possessed an extra opening (foramen) in its skull of unknown function.","It provides evidence for early diplodocoid radiation in North America."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Suuwassea emilieae description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suuwassea"}]

name: Jobaria
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 by Paul Sereno's expedition in the Sahara Desert, Niger.
• Described in 1999 based on numerous well-preserved skeletons.
• The dating of its formation is debated, ranging from Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
interestingFacts: ["It had a relatively short, primitive neck compared to later sauropods.","Its spoon-shaped teeth were adapted for nipping branches.","It was the most common large herbivore in its African environment."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Jobaria tiguidensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jobaria"}]

name: Bellusaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Junggar Basin in Xinjiang, China.
• Described in 1987 by Dong Zhiming.
• Seventeen juvenile skeletons were found together in a single quarry.
interestingFacts: ["The mass grave suggests a herd perished together in a flash flood.","All known specimens are juveniles.","It was a small macronarian sauropod."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Bellusaurus sui description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellusaurus"}]

name: Dryosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1876 in Wyoming and sent to O.C. Marsh.
• Described by Marsh in 1894, meaning 'oak lizard' due to leaf-shaped teeth.
• Skeletons of multiple growth stages have been found.
interestingFacts: ["It was a fast, agile bipedal runner.","It lacked the thumb spikes seen in later iguanodonts.","It was a highly successful, small herbivore of the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dryosaurus altus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryosaurus"}]

name: Camptosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1879 by William Harlow Reed in Wyoming.
• Named by O.C. Marsh in 1885.
• It is commonly found in association with Stegosaurus remains.
interestingFacts: ["It was a heavily built ornithopod that could walk on two or four legs.","It possessed a small, hooved thumb on its hands.","Its beak was toothless, but it had tightly packed cheek teeth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Camptosaurus dispar description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camptosaurus"}]

name: Kentrosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during the German expeditions to the Tendaguru Formation, Tanzania (1909–1912).
• Described by Edwin Hennig in 1915.
• Hundreds of bones were excavated, allowing for detailed reconstruction.
interestingFacts: ["Its back was covered in pairs of plates that transitioned into long spikes near the tail.","It featured a prominent spike pointing backward from each shoulder.","It was smaller and more primitively built than Stegosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Kentrosaurus aethiopicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentrosaurus"}]

name: Scutellosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1971 in the Kayenta Formation, Arizona.
• Described in 1981 by E.H. Colbert.
• Hundreds of small osteoderms (armor plates) were found with the skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest known armored dinosaurs.","It was a small, lightly built, bipedal herbivore.","Its body was covered in parallel rows of small bony scutes."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scutellosaurus lawleri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutellosaurus"}]

name: Scelidosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1858 at Charmouth, England, by James Harrison.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1861.
• Exceptionally complete specimens have been recovered from marine deposits.
interestingFacts: ["It was covered in rows of keeled bony armor.","It is considered an early relative of both ankylosaurs and stegosaurs.","It was a quadrupedal browser with a small head and leaf-shaped teeth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scelidosaurus harrisonii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scelidosaurus"}]

name: Gargoyleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 in the Bone Cabin Quarry West, Wyoming.
• Named in 1998 by Ken Carpenter and colleagues.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete, well-preserved skull.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest and most complete known ankylosaurs.","Its heavily armored skull had prominent horns on the rear corners.","It had a complex network of nasal passages."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gargoyleosaurus parkpinorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyleosaurus"}]

name: Othnielosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the late 19th century and heavily revised over time.
• Named in 2007 by Peter Galton to replace the confused taxon Othnielia.
• Known from several partial skeletons in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: ["It was a small, swift, bipedal herbivore.","It possessed enameled teeth well-adapted to chewing tough vegetation.","Its name honors paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Othnielosaurus consors description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othnielosaurus"}]

name: Lesothosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Lesotho in the upper Elliot Formation.
• Described by Peter Galton in 1978.
• The holotype includes partial skull and postcranial material.
• Originally thought to be an ornithopod, later recognized as a basal ornithischian.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest known ornithischian dinosaurs.","It had a small, slender body built for fast running.","Its teeth were leaf-shaped, adapted for slicing plant material."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Lesothosaurus diagnosticus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesothosaurus"}]

name: Hexinlusaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils found in the Lower Shaximiao Formation, China.
• Described originally as a species of Yandusaurus in 1983.
• Reclassified and named Hexinlusaurus by Barrett et al. in 2005.
• Name honors Professor He Xinlu.
interestingFacts: ["A small, basal neornithischian dinosaur.","It had prominent ridges on its teeth for grinding.","Coexisted with larger dinosaurs like Shunosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Hexinlusaurus multidens description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexinlusaurus"}]

name: Chialingosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Upper Shaximiao Formation in Sichuan, China in 1957.
• Described by C.C. Young in 1959.
• One of the first stegosaurs discovered in China.
• The holotype is based on fragmentary remains.
interestingFacts: ["It was a very slender and primitive stegosaur.","Named after the Jialing River in Sichuan.","Its plates were narrower and more spine-like compared to later stegosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Chialingosaurus kuani description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chialingosaurus"}]

name: Tuojiangosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Upper Shaximiao Formation of Sichuan, China in 1977.
• Described by Dong Zhiming and colleagues.
• Best-known Asian stegosaur, with a nearly complete skeleton.
• Named after the Tuo River.
interestingFacts: ["Featured 15 pairs of pointed plates along its back.","Had a distinctive pair of spikes on its shoulders.","Bore a thagomizer with four large spikes at the end of its tail."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Tuojiangosaurus multispinus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuojiangosaurus"}]

name: Dacentrurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in England in 1874.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1875, originally as Omosaurus.
• Renamed Dacentrurus in 1902 by Frederic Lucas.
• Was the very first stegosaur ever discovered.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed paired spikes rather than plates along most of its back and tail.","Its front limbs were relatively long for a stegosaur.","The pelvis was exceptionally broad to accommodate a large gut."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dacentrurus armatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacentrurus"}]

name: Miragaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lourinhã Formation, Portugal.
• Described by Octávio Mateus and colleagues in 2009.
• The holotype consists of the front half of a skeleton, notably the neck.
• Named after the Portuguese parish of Miragaia.
interestingFacts: ["Had an unusually long neck with at least 17 vertebrae.","Its neck length rivaled some sauropods.","Its back was adorned with paired triangular plates."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Miragaia longicollum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miragaia"}]

name: Hesperosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, USA, in 1985.
• Described by Kenneth Carpenter in 2001.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skull and much of the skeleton.
• Its name means western lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Closely related to Stegosaurus but had broader, oval-shaped plates.","Its skull was proportionately wider than that of Stegosaurus.","Lived slightly earlier than most Stegosaurus species."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Hesperosaurus mjosi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesperosaurus"}]

name: Fruitadens
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in the 1970s.
• Described by Richard Butler and colleagues in 2010.
• The name means Fruita tooth, after the Fruita Paleontological Area.
• Represented by remains of multiple individuals.
interestingFacts: ["One of the smallest known ornithischian dinosaurs.","Had canine-like tusks in its lower jaw.","Likely an omnivore, eating both plants and small animals or insects."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Fruitadens haagarorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruitadens"}]

name: Nanosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
• Described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
• Historically a taxonomic wastebasket taxon.
• Recent studies have clarified its classification among early ornithischians.
interestingFacts: ["A small, agile, bipedal dinosaur.","Othnielosaurus is often considered a synonym of Nanosaurus.","Used speed to escape from contemporary predators like Allosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Nanosaurus agilis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanosaurus"}]

name: Rhamphorhynchus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
• First named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1847.
• Known from numerous perfectly preserved specimens.
• Many specimens preserve soft tissues, including wing membranes.
interestingFacts: ["Had a long, stiff tail ending in a diamond-shaped vane.","Its jaws were filled with sharp, forward-pointing teeth for catching fish.","Lacked a bony crest on its head."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Rhamphorhynchus muensteri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhamphorhynchus"}]

name: Dimorphodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Dorset, England, in 1828.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1859.
• One of the first pterosaurs ever found.
• Name means two-form tooth, referring to its differentiated teeth.
interestingFacts: ["Had a remarkably large, deep skull resembling that of a puffin.","Possessed two distinct types of teeth in its jaws.","Its wings were relatively short, suggesting it was not an oceanic soarer."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dimorphodon macronyx description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimorphodon"}]

name: Pterodactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
• Described by Cosimo Alessandro Collini in 1784.
• The first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile.
• Georges Cuvier later coined the name Ptero-dactyle.
interestingFacts: ["Had a long, pointed beak filled with small teeth.","It was a short-tailed pterosaur (pterodactyloid).","Likely fed on small fish and invertebrates."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pterodactylus antiquus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterodactylus"}]

name: Anurognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Ludwig Döderlein in 1923.
• The holotype is a small, nearly complete skeleton on a single slab.
• Its name means without tail and jaw.
interestingFacts: ["Had a very short skull and broad, frog-like mouth.","Unlike its relatives, it had a very short tail.","Likely an aerial insectivore, similar to modern nightjars."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Anurognathus ammoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anurognathus"}]

name: Scaphognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• First described by August Goldfuss in 1831.
• Originally assigned to Pterodactylus before getting its own genus.
• Only a few specimens have ever been found.
interestingFacts: ["Had a broader, more robust skull than its relative Rhamphorhynchus.","Its teeth were vertically oriented rather than pointing forward.","Its brain was relatively large compared to other early pterosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scaphognathus crassirostris description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaphognathus"}]

name: Sordes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Karabastau Formation of Kazakhstan in 1971.
• Described by Aleksandr Grigorevich Sharov.
• The holotype prominently preserved impressions of hair-like structures (pycnofibers).
• The name Sordes pilosus means hairy devil.
interestingFacts: ["Provided the first undeniable proof that pterosaurs were covered in fluff.","Had a thick coat of pycnofibers over its body and part of its wings.","Was a small, long-tailed pterosaur."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sordes pilosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sordes"}]

name: Darwinopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2009.
• Named in honor of Charles Darwin on the 200th anniversary of his birth.
• Represented by numerous complete skeletons, including one with an egg.
interestingFacts: ["A crucial missing link showing modular evolution in pterosaurs.","Had a long tail like early pterosaurs, but the skull of advanced ones.","Exhibited clear sexual dimorphism, with males having head crests."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Darwinopterus modularis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwinopterus"}]

name: Wukongopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2009.
• Named after Sun Wukong, the Monkey King from Chinese mythology.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Part of the transitional group connecting basal and advanced pterosaurs.","Had a robust tail and elongated cervical vertebrae.","Likely arboreal, navigating through dense forest environments."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Wukongopterus lii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wukongopterus"}]

name: Kunpengopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of China.
• Described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2010.
• Named after the Kunpeng, a mythical Chinese creature that transforms from fish to bird.
• Known from well-preserved specimens including an egg.
interestingFacts: ["Recently discovered to possess an opposable thumb.","The opposable thumb suggests it lived and climbed in trees.","It lacked a bony crest on its head."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Kunpengopterus sinensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunpengopterus"}]

name: Ctenochasma
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1852.
• Its name means comb jaw.
• Found primarily in late Jurassic marine deposits.
interestingFacts: ["Had hundreds of long, thin teeth forming a comb-like structure.","Used its unique jaws to filter-feed on small aquatic organisms.","Was a fully flying equivalent to modern flamingos."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ctenochasma roemeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ctenochasma"}]

name: Gnathosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Hermann von Meyer in 1833.
• Was originally mistaken for a teleosaurid (marine crocodile).
• Reidentified as a pterosaur by Albert Oppel in 1862.
interestingFacts: ["Its jaws broadened at the tip into a spoon-like shape.","Possessed over 130 needle-like teeth.","Fed by sweeping its jaws through mud to catch small invertebrates."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gnathosaurus subulatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnathosaurus"}]

name: Cycnorhamphus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone in Germany.
• First named in 1855, but later lumped with Pterodactylus.
• Reinstated as a distinct genus in the mid-20th century.
• Name means swan beak.
interestingFacts: ["Had unusual jaws with a distinctive upward curve or kink.","Likely used its specialized jaws to crush hard-shelled prey.","Lacked teeth in the front portion of its mouth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cycnorhamphus suevicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycnorhamphus"}]

name: Germanodactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Originally assigned to Pterodactylus in 1901.
• Reclassified as its own genus by C.C. Young in 1964.
• Name means German finger.
interestingFacts: ["Had a prominent bony crest running along the top of its skull.","Its jaws were mostly toothless at the very front.","Likely hunted fish, similar to modern terns."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Germanodactylus cristatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanodactylus"}]

name: Pterorhynchus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Stephen Czerkas and Ji Qiang in 2002.
• Only one well-preserved specimen has been found.
• The name means wing snout.
interestingFacts: ["Preserved an intricate, sail-like crest made of keratin.","Had long hair-like pycnofibers with distinct tufts.","Its tail vane was reinforced by elongated scales."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pterorhynchus wellnhoferi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterorhynchus"}]

name: Harpactognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, USA.
• Described by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues in 2003.
• Known only from a partial snout.
• Name means snatching jaw.
interestingFacts: ["One of the few large pterosaurs known from the Morrison Formation.","Had a significant bony crest extending to the tip of its snout.","Its wingspan is estimated to have been around 2.5 meters."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Harpactognathus gentryii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpactognathus"}]

name: Mesadactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
• Described by James Jensen and Kevin Padian in 1989.
• Known from fragmentary remains, primarily a synsacrum.
• Name means Mesa finger, after the discovery site at Dry Mesa Quarry.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest recognized pterodactyloid pterosaurs in North America.","Was quite small, with an estimated wingspan under 1 meter.","Its isolated bones were initially confused with bird remains."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Mesadactylus ornithosphyos description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesadactylus"}]

name: Jianchangnathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Xin Cheng and colleagues in 2012.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton.
• Closely related to the genus Scaphognathus.
interestingFacts: ["Had a highly robust lower jaw with a prominent chin.","Only three teeth were present in each maxilla.","Its tail was relatively straight and rigid."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Jianchangnathus robustus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jianchangnathus"}]

name: Fenghuangopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2010.
• Represented by a single, beautifully preserved skeleton.
• Named after the Fenghuang, a mythological Chinese bird.
interestingFacts: ["A member of the scaphognathine group of pterosaurs.","Had a blunt, short skull packed with vertically oriented teeth.","Provides key insights into early pterosaur diversity in Asia."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Fenghuangopterus lii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenghuangopterus"}]

name: Liopleurodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England or France.
• Described by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
• Name means smooth-sided tooth, referring to its tooth enamel.
• Gained fame through its exaggerated depiction in Walking with Dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["A formidable apex predator of the Jurassic seas.","Though famously portrayed as 25 meters long, it actually reached about 6-7 meters.","Had an exceptionally powerful bite force."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Liopleurodon ferox description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liopleurodon"}]

name: Plesiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in 1823.
• Described by William Conybeare in 1824.
• The first complete plesiosaur skeleton ever found.
• Its name means near lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by a small head, long neck, and four large flippers.","Moved through the water by flying with its flippers, like modern sea turtles.","Its diet consisted mainly of fish and small cephalopods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Plesiosaurus dolichodeirus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plesiosaurus"}]

name: Ichthyosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in the early 19th century.
• Described by Charles König in 1818.
• The first fully recognized genus of the ichthyosaur group.
• Its name translates to fish lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Convergent evolution gave it a body shape strikingly similar to a modern dolphin.","Gave birth to live young at sea, as proven by fossilized mothers with embryos.","Had massive eyes reinforced by bony rings for deep-water vision."]

name: Ophthalmosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• Hundreds of specimens have been discovered worldwide.
• The name means eye lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Had the largest eyes relative to body size of any known vertebrate.","Its enormous eyes suggest it hunted in deep, dark waters.","Possessed a teardrop-shaped body built for high-speed swimming."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ophthalmosaurus icenicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophthalmosaurus"}]

name: Cryptoclidus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1892.
• Name means hidden collarbone, referring to its small clavicles.
• Known from numerous excellent skeletons.
interestingFacts: ["Had a surprisingly fragile skull for a marine predator.","Its jaws were lined with dozens of interlocking, needle-like teeth.","Likely fed by trapping small fish and soft-bodied squid."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cryptoclidus eurymerus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptoclidus"}]

name: Rhomaleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Alum Shale Formation of Yorkshire, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• The most famous specimen is named the Barrow Kipper.
• Name means strong lizard.
interestingFacts: ["A large, robust pliosaur with a powerful build.","Had an internal nasal passage that allowed it to smell underwater.","Hunted other large marine reptiles as well as big fish."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Rhomaleosaurus cramptoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhomaleosaurus"}]

name: Macroplata
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Blue Lias Formation in Warwickshire, England.
• Described by William Elgin Swinton in 1930.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skeleton.
• Its name means big plate, referring to its large shoulder bones.
interestingFacts: ["Had an unusually long neck for an early pliosaur.","Its skull was robust and crocodilian in shape.","Reached about 4.5 meters in length."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Macroplata tenuiceps description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroplata"}]

name: Peloneustes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The name translates roughly to mud swimmer.
• Known from numerous specimens.
interestingFacts: ["A relatively small pliosaur, measuring around 3 meters long.","Had fewer, more robust teeth than its relatives.","Specialized in hunting hard-shelled prey like ammonites and belemnites."]

name: Pliosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It is the type genus for the entire group of short-necked plesiosaurs.
• The famous Predator X was eventually classified as a species of Pliosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["An enormous apex predator of the Late Jurassic.","Its skull could reach over 2 meters in length.","Its bite force was powerful enough to crush a car."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pliosaurus brachydeirus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliosaurus"}]

name: Simolestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England in the 19th century.
• Described by Charles William Andrews in 1909.
• Name means snub-nosed thief.
• A very complete skeleton was found in a brick pit in Peterborough.
interestingFacts: ["Had a remarkably short, blunt snout.","Its jaw muscles were exceptionally large, giving it a very powerful bite.","Likely specialized in twisting chunks of flesh off large prey."]

name: Temnodontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The first ichthyosaur skull ever found belonged to this genus.
• Name means cutting-tooth lizard.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest known ichthyosaurs, reaching up to 12 meters.","An apex predator that fed on other marine reptiles and large cephalopods.","Possessed large, robust teeth with distinct cutting edges."]

name: Excalibosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lower Lias of Somerset, England, in 1984.
• Described by Christopher McGowan in 1986.
• Named after Excalibur, King Arthur legendary sword.
• Known from a nearly complete skeleton.

name: Morganucodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in limestone fissures in Glamorgan, Wales, in 1941.
• Described by Walter Kühne in 1949.
• Its name means Glamorgan tooth.
• Thousands of isolated teeth and bones have since been found.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest and most transitional forms between cynodonts and true mammals.","Had a double jaw joint, a hallmark of early mammalian evolution.","Was a tiny, shrew-like animal that hunted insects at night."]

name: Castorocauda
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China, in 2004.
• Described by Qiang Ji and colleagues in 2006.
• Preserved remarkably detailed impressions of hair and soft tissue.
• Name means beaver tail.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known mammal-like animal with a beaver-like tail and webbed feet.","Provides evidence that early mammaliaforms were highly specialized, not just generalized shrews.","Preserves the oldest known evidence of mammalian hair."]

name: Volaticotherium
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.

• Name means ancient gliding beast.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known gliding mammal-like animal.","Pushed back the origin of mammalian gliding flight by 70 million years.","Had sharp teeth adapted for a purely insectivorous diet."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Volaticotherium antiquum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volaticotherium"}]

name: Fruitafossor
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in 2005.

• Nicknamed Popeye due to its massive arm bones.

name: Juramaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
